battle.title: Collections Crash Course
battle.description: Lists, sets and maps under pressure: pick the right tool and survive the traps.

questions.text: Which collection automatically rejects duplicate elements and has no get(index) method?
questions.explanation: A Set holds each element at most once and is not indexed. ArrayList and LinkedList allow duplicates and index access, and ArrayDeque also allows duplicates.
Putting an existing key replaces its value instead of adding an entry, so the map has 2 entries and a is now 3. Expecting 3 entries treats put like a list add.
remove(1) with an int argument removes the element at index 1 (the 20). Then remove(Integer.valueOf(1)) removes the value 1. Thinking remove(1) deletes the value 1 gives the wrong list.

questions.text: You must count how many times each word appears in a text and then print the words in alphabetical order. Which structure fits best?
options: ArrayList<String> with nested loops to count
HashMap<String,Integer> printed in its iteration order
questions.explanation: A map stores a count per word and TreeMap keeps its keys sorted, so iteration is alphabetical. HashMap has no guaranteed order, and a HashSet cannot store counts.

Structurally modifying an ArrayList while a for-each loop iterates it makes the iterator throw ConcurrentModificationException on the next step. Expecting a clean [1, 3, 4] ignores the fail-fast iterator; use Iterator.remove or removeIf instead.

coding.title: Word Frequency Ranking
coding.description: Read n lowercase words. Print each distinct word with the number of times it occurs, one 'word count' pair per line. Order the lines by count from highest to lowest; words with the same count go in alphabetical order.
coding.inputDescription: Line 1: n. Line 2: n words separated by spaces.
coding.outputDescription: One line per distinct word: the word, a space, its count.
coding.constraints: 1 <= n <= 1000, each word has 1 to 10 characters

debug.title: The Wrong Remove
debug.description: The program reads n integers and then a target value, and should remove the first occurrence of that VALUE from the list, then print the remaining numbers separated by spaces. It removes the wrong element or crashes. Input: n, the n integers, then the target (the target is always in the list). Output: remaining numbers on one line.
hints: Run it on '3 2 1' with target 1. Which number disappears and which one should?
Look at the list.remove(...) call. ArrayList has more than one remove method.
remove(int) deletes by position and remove(Object) deletes by value. With an int variable, which one is chosen?
Wrap the target so Java picks the by-value version: list.remove(Integer.valueOf(target)).
